items.q: Few-shot prompting means:
options: Keeping the prompt as short as possible
Supplying worked input–output examples so the pattern is demonstrated
Asking the same question several times and comparing
items.explain: Examples are the pattern already, which skips the lossy step of converting your description into one.

items.q: Which examples are most valuable in a few-shot prompt?
options: Clean, representative ones
The awkward ones — empty fields, ambiguity, cases to refuse
The longest realistic ones
items.explain: The straightforward case usually works unaided. The boundary is where automated work fails.

items.q: The most common cause of 'it mostly works but not reliably':
options: Too few examples
Examples that contradict each other
An underpowered model
items.explain: If one example writes 'none' and another 'N/A', you have demonstrated both are acceptable — and you will get both.

items.q: Why does automation need structured output rather than prose?
options: It is shorter
The next step must find values by key or position, which prose does not provide
Models are more accurate when writing JSON
items.explain: A person extracts facts from a sentence effortlessly; a spreadsheet or automation step ends up guessing.

items.q: Which instruction is most often forgotten in a format specification?
options: Naming the fields
Banning any text outside the structure
Specifying the date format
items.explain: Without it you get "Here's the extracted data:" wrapped around your JSON, and the consumer chokes on the first character.

items.q: When a run returns unparseable output, the worst response is:
options: Retry once, then route to a human
Let it become an empty value that looks like a legitimate 'none'
Log it and raise a visible error
items.explain: That corrupts data silently, which is worse than failing loudly — nobody finds out until the numbers are already wrong.

items.q: Why does one prompt doing five jobs do each one worse?
options: Prompts have a hard length limit
The objectives compete for finite attention and contaminate each other
Models can only follow one instruction at a time
items.explain: Having decided something is urgent, the draft becomes apologetic — and you cannot see the interaction in the final output.

items.q: The clearest signal a prompt is doing too much:
options: It is longer than a paragraph
Describing what it does requires the word 'and'
It contains examples
items.explain: "Summarise the meeting and extract the actions" is two prompts wearing one coat.

items.q: A practical benefit of splitting a prompt, beyond reliability:
options: Cheap models can handle the simple steps
Prompts become shorter to write
Output no longer needs validating
items.explain: Classification can go to a small fast model while only the draft needs a capable one, often making the chain cheaper overall.

items.q: Four chained steps, each 95% accurate, are roughly:
options: 95% accurate end to end
81% accurate end to end
99% accurate end to end
items.explain: Accuracy multiplies rather than averaging, so adding steps costs reliability even when each is individually good.

items.q: Chains fail quietly because:
options: Errors are logged but not surfaced
Each step produces plausible output from whatever it received
Models suppress error messages
items.explain: A misclassification at step one is processed confidently by every later step. The result is coherent, wrong, and does not look wrong.

items.q: A human checkpoint belongs:
options: After every step
Before anything irreversible, and after steps later ones cannot sanity-check
Only at the very end of the chain
items.explain: Checking everything defeats the purpose. Flagged cases plus everything irreversible is what actually scales.

items.q: Between chained steps you should pass:
options: A prose summary of the result
Structured data, and only what the next step needs
The entire conversation so far
items.explain: Prose means every step re-parses natural language. Sending everything also lets irrelevant material influence the next prompt.

items.q: Which belongs in persistent instructions?
options: The specific task you want done
Standing format and language rules you would otherwise retype
The current project's name
items.explain: The test is whether you would write it every time. Tasks and anything that varies belong in the request.

items.q: Instruction drift means:
options: The model is updated and behaves differently
Persistent rules weaken as a conversation grows and competes with them
Stored instructions become corrupted
items.explain: A system prompt sits at the very start of the context. By message forty its influence has faded.

items.q: For an automated chain you should:
options: Rely on a long-running conversation for context
Send every request fresh with its full instructions
Put the task into the system prompt
items.explain: A chain should not depend on conversational history it did not control, and fresh requests avoid drift entirely.

items.q: In a long input, material is used least reliably when it sits:
options: At the beginning
In the middle
At the end
items.explain: Beginning and end are attended to more reliably; a fact buried halfway through is measurably more likely to be missed.

items.q: With a very long document, the instruction is best placed:
options: Before the document, kept brief
After the document, or in both places
In the system prompt only
items.explain: The end of the input is attended to reliably. Repeating it before and after feels inelegant and measurably helps.

items.q: Supplying only the relevant section rather than the whole document:
options: Usually produces worse answers because context is missing
Usually produces better answers and costs less
Makes no measurable difference
items.explain: Relevant material is not diluted and there is less chance of drawing on the wrong part — better quality and lower cost together.

items.q: Why is 'it looks better after my change' unreliable?
options: Models vary between runs
You tested the case you were thinking about, and the change may have broken others
Improvements take time to become visible
items.explain: Adding "be concise" fixes a verbose case and truncates ones that needed detail. Without a fixed set you never see that.

items.q: An evaluation set should be weighted towards:
options: Typical, representative inputs
Edge cases, ambiguity and previously seen failures
The longest inputs you handle
items.explain: A few normal cases catch basic regressions; the edge cases are where automated work actually fails.

items.q: The score from an evaluation set is primarily:
options: A target to maximise
A change detector — did this edit help or hurt?
A measure of the model's quality
items.explain: 20/20 usually means your set is too easy. The value is knowing whether today's edit improved things.

items.q: A prompt that worked for months stops working. Most likely cause:
options: The prompt degraded over time
The model behind it was updated or replaced
The prompt file was corrupted
items.explain: Your prompt sits unchanged in a file. What moves is everything underneath it, and nothing announces the change.

items.q: The most valuable and most often missing part of a prompt handover:
options: The prompt text
The known failures
The author's name
items.explain: Someone who knows the boundary can work around it. Someone who does not will find it in production.
